newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's new government prepares crucial budget.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's new government prepares crucial budget.

text.p: Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's four-month-old government will present its first budget on June 14 in what economists say will be a crucial test of its ability to deal with Pakistan's daunting economic crisis.
With the dollar rising in the unofficial market and stock prices depressed, investors worry that the government might buckle under the strain of gaping current account and fiscal deficits.

Soon after sweeping to power in February 3 polls, Sharif unveiled several incentive packages cutting taxes and import tariffs across the board, but analysts say the budget may withdraw some of these reductions to bridge a yawning revenue gap.
But the Central Board of Revenue on Friday imposed regulatory import duty at 10 to 35 percent on 71 industrial items in a partial reversal of its tariff cut package.
"It seems they had no vision," said a foreign economist of Sharif's economic team. "They had no idea where they want to be and there is certainly no road map."
The economist, who asked not to be named, said the incentive packages were slapped together to try to counter the impact of failed negotiations with the International Monetary Fund.
Pakistan's inability to meet agreed economic targets prompted the IMF to halt a standby loan after Sharif took over.

The IMF is closely monitoring the macroeconomic indicators for fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) and an IMF mission has been at work in Islamabad to set targets for 1997/98 in consultation with Finance Ministry officials preparing the budget.

If the targets are met and the budget proves satisfactory, another IMF team is expected to begin talks in July on a medium-term loan, or enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF), which could be agreed as early as September.

"The impression that there are no (IMF) targets for June 30 is wrong," the economist said, adding that there would be little point in starting ESAF talks in July if most of this year's targets are missed or the government rejects next year's. June 30 is the end of the financial year.
"Delay in ESAF could mean enormous trouble," he said.
Ashfaque Khan, chief economist at the Pakistan Institute of Development Economics, said last week that Pakistan faces debt repayments totalling $2.891 billion in the next six months.
He told a business conference that Pakistan's average monthly trade gap would be $300 million, while foreign reserves, now around $800 million, were unlikely to improve drastically.
"Without IMF support, Pakistan will have a very bad balance of payments situation," he said.

Hafeez Pasha, deputy chairman of the Planning Commission, told the conference the budget would aim to cut the fiscal deficit to five percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from a forecast 6.1 percent in 1996/97.
It would try to reduce the current account deficit to 5.5 percent of GDP from 6.7 percent, while boosting export growth to 11 or 12 percent and keeping imports stable at $12 billion.

Pasha said the targets would be achieved through deep public spending cuts, aggressive export promotion and an expected revival of industrial production that should translate into GDP growth of six percent while cutting inflation to nine percent.
GDP is expected to grow less than three percent in 1996/97 and annual inflation will slightly exceed 12 percent, he said.
However, a senior official of the State (central) Bank of Pakistan said: "We would be happy if GDP growth of five percent with inflation at 12 percent can be achieved (in 1997/98)."

With a narrow export base relying on the vulnerable cotton crop and an expected "The tax and tariff cuts, even if maintained in the budget, are unlikely to show an impact before at least a year," the official said, adding that IMF support would be crucial.
